words: Beautiful. There's certainly a need for mechanics, for good mechanics all over. So it's possible that he could get a skill like that and come back to Yelp River. He'll all kind of like to come back to Yelp River.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It seems like everybody just comes back, you know. Even if you leave for a while, you end up coming back.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I've noticed that. Really?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You know, like they move away for a while. Some people just don't like it, but most people, if they do, if you like it, you stay here, it seems like, and if you don't, you get out. There's no end to it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: The family seems to be important for people that live here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Mm-hmm.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Where did you meet your husband?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Here in Elk River.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Was he a student?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, he was working with the fire patrol.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I see. And he came from Minnesota.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He came from Minnesota in 1970. He worked out here every summer. He'd come out here working summer and he didn't go home. He'd been here three years before I met him. I didn't even know him. It seems strange to me because for every year together you never know him.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: In a small place like this, how could you avoid him? Right. And you met him through a mutual friend?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: My girlfriend got us together.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: How long was your courting period?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Five months.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Five months. So you made up your mind pretty fast.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I made up my mind the first night.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Were you back from your school then?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, I was working in a potlatch.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's when you were working in a potlatch. I see. Now I've got that kind of straight. Had you always planned to get married sometime?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Mm-hmm. I think that's always what I really wanted. I was never really happy living alone. I mean, I was happy and all. I was having a good time.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But you never thought it was a long-term thing?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, I always wanted to settle down and have a baby, it seemed like.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So that you really were kind of looking for a husband all the time?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah. Well, I wasn't really looking for a husband.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But a person you'd like to settle down with. Right. So it was a matter of deciding who it would be.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Meet the right one.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: How do you feel about marriage by now?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I like it. I've never been happier, really.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So it's fulfilled your expectations? Right. About what it would be like. And you're not unhappy about it in any way. Well, we talked a little bit about medical services. And your child was born in Moscow. And we've talked about how you really need something here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, I think we do.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: To make people feel a little more secure.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Sure. Right. Because if somebody gets sick, it's really hard. These roads aren't the best either.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Especially in the wintertime.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Right. In the wintertime, it's really bad. They blew up a helicopter one time.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What's bad is the ones that don't have cars, like your grandma and grandpa.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But then we have us.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And then, well, sometimes it's hard. When we have to go, they can't go. When they can go, we can't go. So you're dependent on them. And I hate to depend on somebody that you depend always. You know, if you do once in a while, it's always you have to depend on them. If we want to go somewhere, we have to depend on them. If we want to go out of town, we have to depend on them. If you want to go across town, church, you have to depend on them. You know, and that's... I kind of like it if we do it for ourselves. I do quite a bit for both of us. It's kind of a wonder. That you like to be independent. I do, as much as possible. My husband don't, but I do. You've got to lean on him. How many children do you want to have?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think two. I kind of have a hard time having kids, so he said only two. I thought about three, but... We'll see what he says. Just next month.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So that probably if you had... Certainly if you had a girl.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yeah. If I had a girl, then that would end it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Have you gotten... You live close to your mother and your grandmother now, so... Any problems about raising children or having babies? Well, you're pretty close to ask questions. Has it worked that way for you?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, yeah, they help. It's really... Because that way I think Eric, he loves them so much, you know. That way I know I'm not alone. I don't have to worry, like, if I have to go someplace, Grandma keeps him, or my mom, or one of the boys, you know. Or, you know, if I don't know something, my mom or grandma's right there to tell me, you know. No, this way should be that way, you know.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You don't have to run Dr. Spock or anything. Right, right. So that's an advantage you have.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's a real advantage, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What do you see as the future for Eric? What would you...have you thought about what you'd like to have him do, or...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You mean like...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's pretty far off.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Once he grows up? Yes. Oh, I don't know. I sort of hope he doesn't work in the woods. But then, you know, I don't want to choose for him. Whatever makes him happy. But we keep thinking we're not... We want to live here, but yet we want to get out so he can see a little more of everything. We'll probably end up living here, and he'll probably go to school here and stuff. But I just...I want him to go to high school and then go on to something else. He knows what he wants. But I don't...I'm not going to push it, you know. There's some people here that have gone to school for five years after high school and still not know what they want to do. So I hope he knows by the time he's a senior in high school what he wants to do.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And so he'll have some choices.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Right. I hope he has, you know, a few ideas on life and stuff. I'm sure he will. I'm sure by then he'll have a lot of ideas we didn't even dream of. Probably lots of occupations will be opened up that we didn't know about, but now, you know.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: How do you see... Do you see the role of children as having changed from the time you were growing up to what... Of course, you haven't had a child very long, and Eric isn't much into his role yet. Do you see any differences in that respect?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The only thing...I don't know if this is how it was when I was little or nothing, but the only thing I noticed is a few of my girlfriends that have babies, you know, they're all constantly comparing. Well, my child is potty trained already and my child can do this and that. I want Eric to see a baby. You know, they're just babies for not very long at all. I don't want to compare him with anybody or anything.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So they're kind of pushing their...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Right. Grow up, grow up, grow up, you know. I want Eric to stay with me.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Do you think it has anything to do with their sense of being a better achievement, being a better mother because their children are potty trained faster than yours?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think so. I talked to my doctor about potty trained talking, you know, and walking and stuff like that. He just says when Eric is ready, he'll let you know. Little kids cannot control their bladder, you know, and stuff like that, so I'm not going to push it. He'll let me know, I think, when he's ready to.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So you think these other mothers have maybe put some stress on their child?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think so. Now, you know, maybe I'm sitting in judgment or something, but I just hope I don't compare him.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He's just bragging to me, you know. Yeah. But the doctor seems to have a sense of this, too. Right. So he's encouraging you just to let Eric go at his own pace. Right. Mm-hmm. What do you do now for, you mentioned some of the things you do for relapsation, recreation with your husband. Is it mostly with your husband? Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But he's got this new job now, so he works longer hours and stuff. So we don't, during the week, we just kind of stay home, and he goes bitter and stuff. But on the weekends, we try to go on a picnic for the last two weekends and take Eric with us. We both like to water ski. Mm-hmm. You know, we both like to go for walks. He really likes to walk out in the woods and look at things. So that's what we do a lot of the time.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's another advantage to being in the outfield, that you're closer to where you can do that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He loves to do that stuff so much. We do that. That's mostly what we do. Because if you want to go to the shower, sometimes you try to clean the moss off.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It gets red. Yeah, you wonder if it's worth all that trip.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Like money and tire gas.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It does take a lot of money, too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Gas and your meals and the show. Mm-hmm. We go once in a while, but not very often.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You have to be pretty sure the show is good enough for that, don't you?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Right, right.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mm-hmm. Is it you— Did your family do things together as you were growing up more, or do you anticipate that you and Eric and his father will do— will there be a change there?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think so. I think we'll probably go more all three of us. Mm-hmm.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: There was a wide variation in your ages with your brothers.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Johnny and I are close, but Jack is five years younger than I am.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did that make a difference?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I can't—you know, I really can't remember too much when I was little, but I can remember Mom and Dad would go in and I'd stand at Grandma's.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I had the kids most of the time, so they went off for their recreation.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Some people just think, you know, I think I'd like the three of us to do stuff together. Mm-hmm. So we'd be there all the time. Did you feel left out? I don't really think I felt left out, but I remember being so lonesome for my Mom and Dad, you know, crying and stuff. Well, really they were probably gone, you know, a few hours downtown or something, you know, but I don't know. I don't think I felt left out as much as I wanted to go, you know, see what they were doing and stuff, maybe. But I wanted to take Eric with us because what we do, he might as well go, you know, and there's no reason to leave him home. Mm-hmm. Because Steve doesn't really enjoy—the only recreation in this town is going to the bar, you know, and Steve doesn't really enjoy that too much, so we don't go down there. We go once in a while. They have the pool tournament, things like that. Grandma babysat every Sunday for that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did he? He played pool? Mm-hmm. He participated?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He liked that real well. Did you? I did. He did too. I did the first few weekends, and then I didn't because it was just mainly guys. It wasn't as much fun as it would have been with a bunch of girls, you know. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Do you enjoy things with other girls now? Uh-huh. You get together, like your birthday clubs and that kind of thing. Mm-hmm. And you just get together socially, I suppose, with others.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Right, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Just mothers and have children and just get together and talk. Uh-huh. Do you ever think about the possibility of what would happen if Steve got injured or hurt or something?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes, I think about the time my girlfriend's husband was killed. They just had a three-month-old baby and stuff. Oh. It just really scared me because Steve was driving over that same road every night. Uh-huh. I think about it. You know, a person doesn't like you, but we have life insurance, and I have my training. I think Eric and I would be all right, you know, even if Steve was injured. Uh-huh. I think I could go to work good enough to support him.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You have something that you can depend on.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Right, I can fall back on it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Some other girls don't have that. Yeah. So that's a benefit for you. Um, what do you think would happen to your relationship with Steve if you ever had to support the family? Would that be disastrous?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think it might for him more than me, I think. You know, I don't think I would resent having to work if something was wrong with him, but I think it would hurt. He went absolutely nuts on his layoff where he was laid up for a long time. I think he would like it because he doesn't have any little hobbies like Grandpa make a basket of stuff to keep busy. Uh-huh. I think he might hurt a little. I don't think, you know, we'd fall apart or anything, but he might take a little bit of adjusting.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It would be kind of damaging to him to have a woman supporting him. Would that be there, too?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I don't know if it would be that so much as he just wouldn't want to be just sitting around the house taking care of the baby and the housework and stuff like that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh-huh. Uh-huh. That isn't what he'd really want to do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, I don't think so. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Um, do you think it would be hard to get a job?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: For me? Uh-huh. I do. It was hard for me getting a job right after school.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Where now I have a little bit of experience, you know, at least.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Right. Right.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But I still think it would be hard. When I went first for a job, you know, the experience and this and that, and I had an application in every doctor's office from here to Pullman, you know. But I think it would be hard, but yeah, I think maybe having a little bit of experience would be my advantage.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: For sure. Uh-huh. Do you ever hear your mother talk about the war years, the depression, your grandmother talk about the depression years?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: My grandma, not my mom so much. Yeah. I hear grandma say it's not the time.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not grandma, no. Do you have advice for her from the depression, what you learned your money? Uh-huh. Anything else?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: A lot of people say, you know, you know it's tough all over. You're going to just have to start scrimping and saving and doing all this. It's hard for us to, you know, we got it, we might as well spend it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: How do you feel about buying on credit?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We don't like that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Do you have, do you tell her anything about that, getting it done? Not really. I haven't said too much to any of them. Unless they come and ask me for advice, then I would give it to them. My opinion, but on my opinion sometimes don't appeal to them. So I say, well, you just have to find out for yourself. Whereas if they fall, they fall hard and they can come back and say, Mom, you was right.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: My mom doesn't like us to ever buy anything on credit because they went through it, I think.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't believe it. The credits I don't believe is this here third party, which is finance. Where if I go buy a stove from Sears and Roebuck, I don't like for them to put on another finance. Let them finance it to themselves. Whereas I bought a secondhand TV. This is what really burned me up. I bought a secondhand TV. I shouldn't say this, maybe. No, that's fine. From, is it alright to name some names? Sure. From the security? Okay, we were agreeing at it. So I bought this TV for $285, which wasn't worth it, but we had to have it. We wanted the TV. Okay, we got the TV. They took our older man for $25, which should have been at least $100, but they only gave us $25, which couldn't help. Come to find out when we had to get it, it was over $300 or more because it went through, oh, I always forget that. Avco? No, the other one. Inofficial? No, they have it all over. I think it kind of went out of commission anyway. And I don't believe, when I was, the first year we were married, John was for everything. We have to have money for this. I said, why? Because we can't pay cash flow, so we'll borrow the money. And I said, where are you going to borrow from? The finance company. Isn't that funny? I can't think of the other finance companies. So I'd write this whole thing, get money, maybe $100. Well, it would take $150 to pay it back. So I got, I said, if we ever get out of debt, I'll never, ever, ever want to go eating with a third party. I just don't like it. You pay $150 for something, you have to pay maybe $250. Well, it's not doing you any good. It's just doing them good. Isn't that crazy? I cannot think of that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We just went and bought a TV and a bed. We've been wanting a new bed. Our bed was 15 years old, and it had it. Just the price brings it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I like to see people, I love Norma June's beautiful furniture. But we can't afford it until we can afford it, like we just have to get along with the old stuff we got. You know? But this year, from buying this secondhand, this has been old, maybe four or five years ago. But when you buy, find out one thing. If you buy a secondhand thing, you're buying somebody else's troubles. There was a reason why they got rid of it. You bet. You bet. That's another thing that's...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Steve really hates to buy a charge or any of that. He always wants to save up the money. That's getting pretty tough to do, though, nowadays, to save up that money and live at the same time for something. And they know it, too. They got you over a barrel. If you want it bad enough, they'll give it to you one way or the other.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So you feel as though you still remember some things from the Depression. Oh, you bet I do. One thing for sure I can remember at Depression time. We had a washing machine, which I needed desperately. I was pregnant with Norma, our middle girl. The other girl was lit real little. And I only had $8 to pay on it. One dollar was as much now as $100 today. Do you know I couldn't scrape enough to get $5 to pay on my washing machine? I asked several people in town. No, they wouldn't give it to you. He made $36 a month. And sometimes you didn't get that. Or I don't know what happened, but I think they just... We just waited and told them that we'd pay it next month, next month, until we finally put $2, $3 on it. And I didn't lose my washing machine. But that's the kind of instant that we were in, you know, at Depression time. And at that time you couldn't get... for everything, to get even a piece of bread and stuff on the table for your children. Really, we only had the one child. Norma, she was born then. And I can remember when she was born. We lived in a little shack. We paid, I think we paid $13 a month, which was, at that time, was pretty hard. And there was a big forest fire out here. And she didn't sleep well, very good. And her dad had to go to work at 3 o'clock in the morning. And she was much fresher like most babies are. And I kept her in the back in the bedroom, and I knelt in the bedroom into the kitchen. And there were cinders on our porch. We went out there at one time, being goodbyed, there were cinders on the front porch. And they come to us and says, if you want to live, if this place, if this town burns up, you want to live, you go, we have to all get together and go up to the river and stay out to the riverbank because to save your life. Well, I had two babies. I just, it was really, and my husband had a frightened fire and stuff, and that was really bad at that time. And, well, and she was only about three months old, three weeks old, I think. And there's a lot of things I can remember. What did you do then? Well, it wasn't, we didn't get that bad. We just, they would go out 3 o'clock in the morning and see my son. He had to go to fight the fire. And, but they finally got it out. It seemed like they didn't have the facility to put out a fire like they do now out in the woods. You know, they drop stuff down and it kind of smothers it. At that time, they didn't have all that stuff. There was an in-power. Well, that's kind of some of the stuff I do remember. I like, I can remember when we first came to Elk River, too. A lot of the stuff that goes on before we ever got to Elk River as far as that's concerned. Well, let's finish up the song before she has to leave for the baby, and then we'll get to your story. I should have said that. No, that's all right. I'm glad you brought it up. Now I'll know how to go, start out to get more of your story. Do you have any, are you involved much in community activities or church activities?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, we go to the Catholic Church in Boulderville. And community activities is Elk River Days, which, you know, there's a lot for Elk River, really. It's on the whole Elk River Days. There's only about four couples that put on the whole Elk River Days. So we really work hard.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What is it, what happens? Is it a festival day, games?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's right, we have parade and flogging and song events and grist hole flying and big bands and what?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You know, motorcycle.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Orgy in Canada, motorcycle races, and big barbecue and a breakfast in the morning, you know, and just a bunch of stuff like that. I wish your grandpa was going to be fast at doing it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think I'll have to try to come down.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It's the third weekend in August. It's the 16th, I think.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You have lots of people here?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They come from all over. Probably old timers even live here. Right, old timers.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's what I'm saying.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You don't have the county fairs out here. Do you have exhibits or any awards that this Elk River Days doesn't have that kind of experience? If you had a friend that you met in San Francisco, one of your friends you met down there, if she married and came to live in Elk River, what would she have to learn to do or what would she have to develop in order to live here and be happy?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: How about the long winters?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yeah, that, oh, yes. Two things, I just take her driving and she probably, the winters aren't, she probably would really freak out in the winters. Doesn't Sharon, because the lights go out and stuff.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Every once in a while when you're unexpected.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Right, for three days sometimes in a row you're out. So I think personally, this one friend of mine, I think she'd love it. She keeps wanting to come out for a visit, but her job keeps her there and stuff, you know. But the town she's from really isn't that big, but it's bigger than Elk, bigger than Moscow and Elk River, you know. I drive in the winters and the logging trucks and the dust, the bad roads and stuff like that, she probably won't have to do. And the people, I think people probably do a lot different than what she's used to.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Is it hard for a stranger to come into the community?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I don't think so, really. It depends on the person. They act friendly and stuff, you know. They give you that chance. I think Elk River's really a warm town as far as greeting strangers.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She'd have to have some way to, kind of things to do for herself, things to do alone.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Right, she'd have to, you know.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Some people in the city kind of develop that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, she'd like this one friend. She's embroidered and stuff like that. I think she'd like it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So you have to kind of have something to do for yourself.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Right, to do. You have to be able to think of stuff. Like a lot of us, we play cards all the time.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You can't run out and go to the movies or some other recreation.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, you can't go out for a nice expensive dinner, bowling.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So you have to learn to live without that. Do you take any magazines on your fingers?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We take the Sunday School for the Nervine, so.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Do you buy magazines?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I sometimes buy the Cosmopolitan, but I don't read them.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not regularly.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I don't subscribe to anything.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Do you watch TV? Mm-hmm. What are your favorite shows?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I like Loda. I like Medical Center and Dr. Welby. I watch the soap opera a lot. Really, by the time we have supper over with and dishes done and Eric's back, I don't want too much to be a night. Maybe there's a day when you're alone with Eric. Maybe when he's taking his meds.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Do you and your husband make decisions together? Is there an area that he makes decisions about, or how do you handle things like that?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think we do make decisions together. We talk it over a lot before we ever make major decisions anyway. Like as far as his job goes, he does that pretty much on his own. He knows what makes him happy and sad.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: How about the spending of the money and everything? Do you both do that?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I keep books. I take a deal from him. We talk it over a bit. I do most of it. Like if we have $20 and I can decide where it goes, I make the decision and he doesn't have to.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He trusts you then, in your judgment. Is there anything that he decides and you wish you had more influence with him on some things or do you just speak up when you...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I just tell him.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So that's just what you would... No.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He doesn't... We can walk through his bars of decision as we take. He doesn't ever just go out and do, you know, buy anything without me with him.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Who decided that you were going to live here in Mount Priebus? Was it his job or...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It was his job. I think we would... If he didn't have a job here, I mean, he could have found one in Pollack. I think he might have lived there the longest. I could have worked a little bit longer, but I don't know. I think it was probably his job. He's worked on the fire patrol at the time and then he got on year-round as a foreman. So we came here. We found a house here before we got married. So... Which means... We both liked it here, you know. That wasn't the only reason we stayed here.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What differences do you see between yourself and the girls who didn't go away to school?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: There's narrow-minded... I'll say that over and over. I've had a lot of things. Narrow-minded and not, you know... I mean, I don't know everything, you know. I didn't live in San Francisco long enough to really know a lot about it. Like, they talk about the city. They don't know, really, what it's like. That's in five days, something. And they don't know what it's like to go on to school. They don't know how hard it is to have to cram a year's work into four months, four hours a day, you know.
